- `setup-modules/shell-env.sh`: Use `{ cmd1; cmd2; } >> file` instead of individual redirects [SC2129] (2 occurrences)
- `setup-modules/core.sh`: Use `{ cmd1; cmd2; } >> file` instead of individual redirects [SC2129] (2 occurrences)

- SC2129: Group multiple redirects to the same file with `{ ...; } >> file`

Ref: quality review issue #2632

title: fix: review-bot-gate passes on rate-limit/quota warnings without actual code review
body:
## Problem

When CodeRabbit or Gemini post rate-limit/quota warning comments on a PR, the `review-bot-gate-helper.sh` reports `PASS` (bots have posted) and the `Wait for AI Review Bots` CI check passes. However, no actual code review occurred — the bots posted error messages, not reviews.

## Observed pattern (2026-03-07)

17 PRs across marcusquinn/aidevops, marcusquinn/aidevops.sh, and marcusquinn/turbostarter-plus all have:
- `review-bot-gate-helper.sh` returning `PASS` (found: coderabbitai gemini-code-assist)
- Formal review count = 0 (no actual reviews)
- CodeRabbit comment: "Rate limit exceeded" 
- Gemini comment: "You have reached your daily quota limit"

The formal review count gate (=0) correctly blocks auto-merge. But the gate check misleadingly reports PASS, which could confuse future pulse logic or human reviewers.

## Root cause

`review-bot-gate-helper.sh` detects bot presence by checking for bot usernames in PR comments. It does not distinguish between rate-limit warnings and actual review comments.

## Proposed fix

In `review-bot-gate-helper.sh`, when a bot comment is found, check whether it contains rate-limit/quota warning patterns (e.g., "Rate limit exceeded", "daily quota limit"). If so, treat it as `WAITING` rather than `PASS` — the bot acknowledged the PR but did not review it.

Alternatively, check for the presence of a CodeRabbit review summary (the `<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: summarize by coderabbit.ai -->` marker combined with actual review content, not just the rate-limit template).

## Impact

Low urgency — the formal review count gate prevents incorrect merges. But the misleading PASS status adds confusion and may cause future pulse logic to incorrectly conclude bots have reviewed when they haven't.

_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟠 Major_

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🌐 Web query:

`GitHub REST API "Get the combined status for a specific reference": does GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/status support pagination via `per_page` and `page`, and what is the default page size?`

💡 Result:

Yes. **GET `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/status`** supports pagination via the standard query parameters **`per_page`** and **`page`** (with **`per_page` max 100**). The **default page size is `per_page=30`** (and **`page` defaults to `1`**). [1]

**Source(s)**  
[1] https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/rest/commits/statuses#parameters-for-get-the-combined-status-for-a-specific-reference

---



</details>

**Add pagination support to the combined-status lookup in the fallback gate check.**

The `gh api` call on line 168 fetches only page 1 of GitHub's combined-status endpoint, which defaults to 30 results per page. Commits with more than 30 statuses will miss matching bot contexts on subsequent pages, causing false negatives. Use `--paginate` with `per_page=100` to fetch all pages, and apply the same fix to `.github/workflows/review-bot-gate.yml`.

The bash example in this section uses `2>/dev/null` to suppress errors from `classify` and `jq` commands. This practice hides valuable debugging information, such as API failures, malformed JSON, or missing dependencies, which goes against the repository's general rules. The `||` construct already handles command failures gracefully. Removing `2>/dev/null` will make this example script more robust and easier to debug without changing its behavior on success.

```markdown
DECOMPOSE_HELPER="$HOME/.aidevops/agents/scripts/task-decompose-helper.sh"

# Only run if the helper exists (t1408.1 must be merged)
if [[ -x "$DECOMPOSE_HELPER" && -n "$TASK_ID" ]]; then
  # Check if subtasks already exist
  EXISTING=$(/bin/bash "$DECOMPOSE_HELPER" classify --task-id "$TASK_ID" --repo-path "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" --quiet) || EXISTING=""
  EXISTING_KIND=$(echo "$EXISTING" | jq -r '.kind // "atomic"' || echo "atomic")

  if [[ "$EXISTING_KIND" == "composite" ]]; then
    EXISTING_SUBS=$(echo "$EXISTING" | jq -r '.existing_subtasks // empty' || echo "")
    if [[ -n "$EXISTING_SUBS" && "$EXISTING_SUBS" != "[]" ]]; then
      # Subtasks already exist — skip decomposition
      echo "[t1408.2] Task $TASK_ID already has subtasks — proceeding with implementation"
    fi
  fi

  # If no existing subtasks, classify the task description
  if [[ -z "$EXISTING_SUBS" || "$EXISTING_SUBS" == "[]" ]]; then
    CLASSIFY=$(/bin/bash "$DECOMPOSE_HELPER" classify --task "$TASK_DESC" --task-id "$TASK_ID" --repo-path "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" --quiet) || CLASSIFY=""
    TASK_KIND=$(echo "$CLASSIFY" | jq -r '.kind // "atomic"' || echo "atomic")
  fi
fi
```

title: t1413: Add memory consolidation phase (cross-memory insight generation)
body:
## Summary

Add a memory consolidation phase to `memory-audit-pulse.sh` that uses a cheap LLM call (haiku-tier, ~$0.001/call) to scan unconsolidated memories, discover cross-cutting connections, and store synthesized insights as new `derives` relations in the existing `learning_relations` table.

## Problem

The existing memory system is maintenance-oriented: dedup removes noise, prune removes staleness, graduate promotes value. But no phase actively **connects** memories to discover patterns. A user who stores "CORS fix: add nginx headers" and later stores "nginx proxy_pass config for API" has two related memories that are never linked.

## Solution

New `phase_consolidate()` in `memory-audit-pulse.sh` (Phase 3.5) that:
1. Queries unconsolidated memories (not yet in any consolidation)
2. Sends batch to `ai-research-helper.sh` (haiku tier) for pattern detection
3. Stores connections as `derives` relations in `learning_relations`
4. Records insights in new `memory_consolidations` table

## Inspired by

Google's [always-on-memory-agent](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/generative-ai/tree/main/gemini/agents/always-on-memory-agent) consolidation loop — adapted to aidevops's batch-oriented architecture (runs in audit pulse, not as a daemon).

generate_sandbox_env() {
	local sandbox_dir="$1"

	if [[ -z "$sandbox_dir" || ! -d "$sandbox_dir" ]]; then
		echo "ERROR: valid sandbox_dir required" >&2
		return 1
	fi

	# Core: override HOME
	printf "export HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}"

	# Preserve REAL_HOME so scripts that need the actual home can find it
	# (e.g., for reading repos.json, which is a framework config not a credential)
	printf "export REAL_HOME=%q\n" "${REAL_HOME}"

	# GH_TOKEN: if set in the current environment, pass it through.

	# The dispatch script is responsible for setting GH_TOKEN before calling this.
	if [[ -n "${GH_TOKEN:-}" ]]; then

	fi

	printf "export XDG_CONFIG_HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.config"
	printf "export XDG_DATA_HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.local/share"

	# Signal to the worker that it's sandboxed (for conditional logic)
	echo "export AIDEVOPS_SANDBOXED=true"
	printf "export AIDEVOPS_SANDBOX_DIR=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}"

	return 0
}

    token="${token//\"/\"\"}"
    if [[ -n "$tokenised_query" ]]; then
        tokenised_query="$tokenised_query \"$token\""

done

🌐 Web query:

`Do GNU coreutils `stat` and macOS/BSD `stat` accept `--` before a pathname, and without `--` will a quoted pathname beginning with `-` still be parsed as an option?`

💡 Result:

Yes for both, and **quoting does not stop option parsing**.

- **GNU coreutils `stat` (GNU/Linux):** coreutils utilities accept `--` to mark the end of options (so a following `-name` is treated as an operand, not an option). The coreutils manual even shows this convention in use (`… mv -t ../d --`).[1] Therefore `stat -- --leading-dash` works, while `stat "-leading-dash"` is still parsed as an option (because quoting doesn’t change the characters seen by `stat`).

- **macOS / BSD `stat`:** BSD `stat` implementations use the standard `getopt()` option parser (e.g., NetBSD’s `stat.c` calls `getopt(argc, argv, options)`).[2] BSD/POSIX `getopt()` treats `--` as the delimiter that ends option processing.[3] POSIX utility syntax guidelines also describe `--` as the way to end options when an operand begins with `-`.[4] So `stat -- --leading-dash` works on macOS/BSD as well, and `stat "-leading-dash"` is still taken as an option.

**Bottom line:** for both GNU and macOS/BSD `stat`, use either:
- `stat -- "$path"` (portable for “path begins with `-`”), or
- `stat "./-leading-dash"` (if it’s a relative pathname).

**Sources:**  
[1] GNU coreutils manual (example using `--` to end options) ([gnu.org](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html))  
[2] NetBSD `stat.c` uses `getopt()` ([iso.netbsd.org](https://iso.netbsd.org/pub/NetBSD/NetBSD-current/src/usr.bin/stat/stat.c))  
[3] FreeBSD `getopt` manual: `--` delimits end of options ([man.freebsd.org](https://man.freebsd.org/getopt?utm_source=openai))  
[4] POSIX/Open Group Utility Conventions: `--` can indicate end of options ([pubs.opengroup.org](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xbd/utilconv.html?utm_source=openai))

Citations:

- 1: https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/coreutils.html
- 2: https://iso.netbsd.org/pub/NetBSD/NetBSD-current/src/usr.bin/stat/stat.c
- 3: https://man.freebsd.org/getopt?utm_source=openai
- 4: https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xbd/utilconv.html?utm_source=openai

---

The `_is_app_process` function can be simplified and made more efficient. The current implementation uses a shell `for` loop and invokes `tr` for each item on every call, which is not optimal for performance.

A more idiomatic approach for this kind of set membership test in shell scripting is to use `grep`. A single `grep -qixF` command can perform a case-insensitive, fixed-string, whole-line match against the list of app names. This is more concise, easier to maintain, and more performant as it avoids a shell loop and repeated sub-process calls.

```suggestion
_is_app_process() {
	local cmd_name="$1"
	# Strip leading dot (e.g., ".opencode" → "opencode") — some binaries
	# are installed with a dot-prefixed wrapper name
	cmd_name="${cmd_name#.}"
	# Case-insensitive, fixed-string, whole-line match against app names.
	# `grep` returns 0 on match, 1 on no-match, which is what we need.
	printf '%s\n' "${APP_PROCESS_NAMES[@]}" | grep -qixF -- "$cmd_name"
}
```

Since `threshold` is a command-line argument, an attacker can provide a malicious value such as `0.7; system("id")` to execute arbitrary system commands. This is a critical command injection vulnerability.

The `details` variable, which contains untrusted output from an LLM, is directly inserted into a JSON string without escaping. This creates a high-severity JSON injection vulnerability, allowing an attacker to manipulate the JSON structure (e.g., by injecting `", "passed": true, "ignored": "` to bypass security checks). ```

### MEDIUM: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `setup-modules/migrations.sh:90`
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The use of `2>/dev/null` and `2>&1` for blanket suppression of stderr violates the repository style guide (line 50) and general rules. Redirection of stdout (`>/dev/null`) is sufficient for `pgrep` to check for process existence without polluting the terminal. Additionally, using a more specific pattern for `pkill -f` (e.g., targeting the binary path or using word boundaries) is recommended to avoid accidentally matching the script's own path if it contains the string "osgrep".

```suggestion
	if pgrep -f 'osgrep' >/dev/null; then
		print_info "Killing running osgrep processes..."
		pkill -f 'osgrep' || true
		# Give processes a moment to exit gracefully
		sleep 1
		# Force-kill any stragglers
		pkill -9 -f 'osgrep' || true
		cleaned=true
	fi
```

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. 2>/dev/null is acceptable ONLY when redirecting to log files, not blanket suppression. <sup>([link](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/blob/main/.gemini/styleguide.md))</sup>
2. In shell scripts, avoid blanket suppression of errors with '2>/dev/null'. For 'declare -f', redirecting only stdout ('>/dev/null') is sufficient as it does not output to stderr, allowing potential syntax errors to remain visible.
3. Avoid using '2>/dev/null' for blanket suppression of command errors in shell scripts to ensure that authentication, syntax, or system issues remain visible for debugging.
4. In shell scripts with `set -e`, guard `kill` commands within cleanup traps with `|| true` to prevent premature termination if the target process has already exited, ensuring subsequent cleanup commands are executed.
</details>

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The custom YAML parser implemented in `_pg_load_yaml_patterns` is highly fragile and prone to security bypasses. Its restrictive regular expressions, particularly for `description` and `pattern` fields, fail to account for valid YAML variations like trailing comments, different quoting styles, or escaped characters. This can lead to critical patterns not being loaded as expected, creating a false sense of security. It is strongly recommended to use a robust, dedicated YAML parser like `yq` or to significantly harden the regex patterns, for example, by using negated character sets like `[^"*]` instead of greedy matches (`.+`) for quoted strings.

The `cmd_scan_stdin` function reads the entire content of stdin into a shell variable using `content=$(cat)`. This approach is vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) via memory exhaustion if the input is excessively large. Since this tool is designed to process untrusted external content (as noted in the script's comments), it should handle large inputs gracefully, either by limiting the maximum input size or by processing the stream in chunks.

The internal data flow in `_pg_scan_patterns_from_stream` constructs a pipe-delimited string by concatenating untrusted data (`matched_text`) directly into the output: `echo "${severity}|${category}|${description}|${matched_text}"`. If the matched text from the untrusted message contains pipe characters (`|`) or newlines, it will corrupt the internal data format. This can be exploited to trick the severity assessment logic (e.g., by injecting a fake `CRITICAL` finding) or to perform log injection in the `_pg_log_attempt` function. All untrusted data should be sanitized or escaped (e.g., by removing or encoding delimiters and newlines) before being included in delimited formats.

## Unactioned Review Feedback

### HIGH: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/sandbox-exec-helper.sh:174`
![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

Executing a command via `bash -c "$command"` where `$command` is constructed from `"$*"` is a significant security risk and bug.

1.  **Bug**: It breaks commands with arguments that contain spaces. For example, `... run my-cmd --path "/path with spaces/"` will fail because the quotes are lost during the `"$*"` expansion.
2.  **Security Risk**: It's vulnerable to command injection. If arguments are not quoted perfectly by the caller, they can be interpreted by the shell. This is equivalent to using `eval` on user input, which is dangerous, especially for a sandbox script.

To fix this, the script should handle the command and its arguments as an array, not a single string. This requires a few changes:

1.  In `sandbox_run`, change the argument parsing to capture all arguments after options into an array, e.g., `local -a cmd_args=()`. The `*)` and `--)` cases in your `while` loop should become `cmd_args=("$@"); break`.
2.  Replace `bash -c "$command"` with direct execution of the array: `"${cmd_args[@]}"`.
3.  Update checks like `[[ -z "$command" ]]` to `[[ ${#cmd_args[@]} -eq 0 ]]`.
4.  Update logging to handle the array, e.g., `log_execution "${cmd_args[*]}" ...`.

This change makes the script much more robust and secure by avoiding an unnecessary layer of shell interpretation.

1. Use bash arrays for dynamic command construction to avoid duplicating argument expansion patterns (e.g., safe expansion for empty arrays) across conditional branches like sudo vs non-sudo paths.

The `log_execution` function manually constructs JSON log entries using `printf` and `sed`, which is highly error-prone and leads to significant security vulnerabilities. The current escaping logic (`sed 's/"/\\"/g'`) is insufficient, failing to properly handle backslashes or newlines. This can result in:
1.  **JSON Injection**: A trailing backslash in the command can escape the closing quote of the `cmd` field, corrupting the JSON structure and allowing injection of other fields.
2.  **Log Injection**: Literal newlines in the command can be written directly, enabling an attacker to inject spoofed log entries that appear valid.
Using a robust JSON tool like `jq` (already a dependency) is crucial to ensure all characters are correctly escaped and formatted, preventing these injection attacks and ensuring the integrity of the audit log.

```suggestion
    # Use jq to safely generate the JSON log entry
    local log_entry
    log_entry=$(jq -n \
        --arg ts "$timestamp" \
        --arg cmd "$logged_cmd" \
        --argjson exit "$exit_code" \
        --argjson duration "$duration" \
        --argjson timeout "$timeout_used" \
        --argjson network_blocked "$network_blocked" \
        --arg passthrough "$passthrough_vars" \

```

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The current implementation to get aggregate diff stats using `git diff --shortstat f\"{hash_list[-1]}~1..{hash_list[0]}\"` will fail if the oldest commit in the session's time window (`hash_list[-1]`) is a root commit (i.e., has no parent). In this case, `~1` is an invalid reference, `git` will return an error, and the script will silently fail to collect diff stats for that session.

To make this more robust, you can check if the oldest commit has a parent. If not, you can diff against git's "empty tree" hash (`4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904`) to correctly capture the changes from the initial commit onwards.

```python
        hash_list = [c["hash"] for c in commits]
        oldest_commit = hash_list[-1]
        newest_commit = hash_list[0]

        # Check if the oldest commit in the range is a root commit (has no parent).
        parent_check = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "-C", repo_path, "rev-parse", "--verify", "--quiet", f"{oldest_commit}^"],
            capture_output=True,
        )

        if parent_check.returncode == 0:
            # Parent exists, diff from parent of oldest commit.
            from_commit = f"{oldest_commit}~1"
        else:
            # No parent, it's a root commit. Diff from the empty tree.
            from_commit = "4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904"

        stat_result = subprocess.run(
            [
                "git", "-C", repo_path, "diff", "--shortstat",
                from_commit,
                newest_commit,
            ],
            capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=15,
        )
```

This state cleanup logic has a bug that can lead to data corruption. The `jq` filter removes entries from `.labeled_issues` based only on the issue number (`select(.issue != $issue)`). **File**: `.agents/scripts/security-helper.sh:584`
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Suppressing stderr for the `skill-scanner` command can hide important errors, such as issues with the Python environment, missing dependencies, or syntax errors in the scanner script itself. This could lead to silent failures where a skill is reported as having "0 findings" when in reality the scan never ran correctly. It would be better to capture stderr and report it if the scan fails.

I suggest redirecting stderr to a file and then checking it in the collection loop. For example, you could change this line to use the suggestion below, and then add this to the collection loop around line 596:
```bash
			if [[ -s "$scan_tmpdir/$i.err" ]]; then
				echo -e "${RED}Error scanning skill '${scan_names[$i]}':${NC}" >&2
				cat "$scan_tmpdir/$i.err" >&2
			fi
```
This will make debugging much easier if a scan fails.

```suggestion
			$scanner_cmd scan "$scan_target" --format json >"$scan_tmpdir/$scan_index.json" 2>"$scan_tmpdir/$scan_index.err" &
```

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. Avoid using '2>/dev/null' for blanket suppression of command errors in shell scripts to ensure that authentication, syntax, or system issues remain visible for debugging.
</details>

Suppressing stderr from `jq` can hide errors if the `$skill_sources` file contains malformed JSON. While the script checks if the file exists, it doesn't validate its content. If `jq` fails, the `while` loop will silently do nothing, and the script will report 0 skills scanned, which could be misleading. It's better to let `jq` errors be visible to aid in debugging malformed `skill-sources.json` files. Since `set -e` is active, the script will exit on a `jq` error, which is appropriate for this kind of failure.

```

1. When reporting errors for failed file operations in shell scripts, such as 'jq' writes, include the file path in the error message. Avoid suppressing stderr with '2>/dev/null' to ensure that diagnostic information about malformed files or write failures is visible.

The pattern of checking for a script's existence and then executing it is repeated for `generate-claude-commands.sh`, `generate-claude-agents.sh`, and `subagent-index-helper.sh`. This duplication also exists in the `update_opencode_config` function.

# Helper function (could be placed at top of file)
_run_generator() {
    local script_path="$1"
    local info_msg="$2"
    local success_msg="$3"
    local failure_msg="$4"
    shift 4
    local script_args=("$@")

    if [[ ! -f "$script_path" ]]; then
        print_warning "Generator script not found: $script_path"
        return
    fi

    print_info "$info_msg"
    if bash "$script_path" "${script_args[@]}"; then
        print_success "$success_msg"
    else
        print_warning "$failure_msg"
    fi

    return 0
}

**`curl | bash` with an unversioned `latest` URL is a supply-chain risk in an automated provisioning context.**

Because `bash: true` is enabled in this subagent's frontmatter, AI workers can execute the shell code blocks directly. ### HIGH: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/config-helper.sh:192`
![security-high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-high-priority.svg) ![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The `dotpath` variable, derived from CLI arguments, is directly interpolated into a `jq` filter string within double quotes. In bash, double quotes allow command substitution (`$(...)`) and variable expansion. An attacker providing a malicious `dotpath` can achieve arbitrary command execution on the host system. For example, a `dotpath` like `$(id)` would trigger the execution of the `id` command.

To remediate this, avoid direct interpolation of variables into shell commands. Use `jq`'s `--arg` or `--argjson` flags to pass data safely to the `jq` process. For dynamic paths, you can use JQ's `getpath` or `path` functions combined with `split(".")`.

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. In shell scripts, use `jq --arg` for strings and `--argjson` for other JSON types (like numbers) to safely pass variables into a `jq` filter. This avoids syntax errors if the variables contain special characters.
</details>

Remediation: Use `jq --arg` to pass the value safely to the `jq` process instead of interpolating it into the command string.

  private generateId(): string {

      id = Array.from(bytes)

        .join("");
    } while (this.pending.has(id));

## Node.js official-doc best practices (production): `uncaughtException` & `unhandledRejection`

### `process.on('uncaughtException', …)`
- Treat it as **last-resort** handling only; Node.js explicitly warns it’s **not safe to resume normal operation** after an uncaught exception. ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html))  
- Use it only to do **synchronous, best-effort cleanup** (close file descriptors/handles, flush logs synchronously) and then **shut down** (typically exit / stop accepting new work). ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html))  
- Rely on an **external supervisor/monitor** (systemd, Kubernetes, PM2, etc.) to restart the process reliably (even if the event is never emitted). ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html))  

### `process.on('unhandledRejection', …)`
- Don’t leave Promise rejections unhandled; Node notes that **not handling Promise rejections is deprecated** and documents `unhandledRejection`/`rejectionHandled` as the mechanism for tracking these cases. ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html))  
- In current Node behavior, if an `unhandledRejection` occurs and **is not handled**, it can be **raised as an uncaught exception** (process-fatal by default behavior). ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html))  

### Control runtime behavior with `--unhandled-rejections`
- Node provides `--unhandled-rejections=mode` to define what happens on unhandled rejections; since Node v15, the documented default is **`throw`** (i.e., it becomes an uncaught exception if you don’t handle the event). ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html))  

### Practical production rule of thumb (aligned with the above)
- **Log + fail fast** on `uncaughtException` / truly unhandled rejections, and let a supervisor restart the process; **prevent them** by handling errors at the source (try/catch around `await`, `.catch()`, framework error middleware). ([nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html))

-	if [[ -d "$target_dir" ]]; then

+	if [[ -f "$skill_file" ]]; then

This logic for installing Python via `uv` has two issues:

1.  **Error Suppression**: `uv python install 3.11 2>/dev/null` hides important error messages from the user, making it hard to debug if the installation fails (e.g., due to network or permission issues). The `2>/dev/null` should be removed.
2.  **Missing Failure Feedback**: If `uv` successfully installs Python but the subsequent verification fails, the script continues without informing the user why the process failed overall. This can be confusing.

Please update this block to remove the error suppression and add feedback for both successful and failed installation attempts.

```shell
	# 3. If uv is available, install Python 3.11 and retry
	if command -v uv &>/dev/null; then
		print_info "No Python >= 3.10 found. Installing Python 3.11 via uv..."
		if uv python install 3.11; then
			# uv installs to its managed path; check if python3.11 is now available
			if command -v python3.11 &>/dev/null && _python_version_ok python3.11; then
				print_success "Python 3.11 installed via uv"
				return 0
			fi
			# uv may have installed it but not on PATH — check uv's python path
			local uv_py
			uv_py=$(uv python find 3.11 2>/dev/null) || true
			if [[ -n "$uv_py" ]] && _python_version_ok "$uv_py"; then
				print_success "Python 3.11 installed via uv (at $uv_py)"
				return 0
			fi
			print_warning "uv installed Python, but verification failed. Please check your uv setup."
		else
			print_warning "uv failed to install Python. Please try manually."
		fi
	fi
```

### HIGH: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/session-miner-pulse.sh:22`
![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The replacement of `dirname` with parameter expansion introduces a bug in an edge case. When the script is invoked without a path prefix (e.g., from a directory in `$PATH`, or with `bash script.sh` from the same directory), `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` will not contain a `/`.

In this scenario, `${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}` evaluates to the script name itself. The `cd` command will then fail as it attempts to change directory into a file, not a directory. Because `set -e` is active, this will cause the script to exit. For example, if the script is run as `session-miner-pulse.sh`, this line becomes `cd "session-miner-pulse.sh" && pwd`, which will fail.

The original `dirname "session-miner-pulse.sh"` would correctly return `.` and the command would succeed.

To robustly get the script's directory using only shell built-ins, you need to handle this case explicitly. I'd recommend a more readable multi-line approach for clarity, which would replace the single line:

```bash
dir="${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}"
if [[ "$dir" == "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" ]]; then
  dir="."
fi
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$dir" && pwd)"
```

This correctly handles all invocation methods while adhering to the goal of removing external command dependencies.

![security-high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-high-priority.svg) ![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The `cmd_clean` function iterates over all worktrees returned by `git worktree list`. It does not distinguish between the main worktree and linked worktrees. If the main worktree is currently on a branch that has been merged (and is not the default branch), the script will proceed to "clean up" heavy directories like `node_modules`, `.next`, and `.turbo` using `rm -rf` before attempting to remove the worktree. While `git worktree remove` will fail for the main worktree, the `rm -rf` commands will succeed, leading to the loss of build artifacts and dependencies in the main repository. 

**Remediation:** The script should identify and skip the main worktree. This can be done by checking if the worktree path is the same as the base repository path or by skipping the first entry in the `git worktree list --porcelain` output.

**Guard against future/corrupted timestamps to prevent indefinite scan suppression.**

The `check_scan_interval()` function at line 1000 validates that `last_run` is numeric, but does not validate it against the current time. If the state file becomes corrupted with a future epoch (or clock skew occurs), `elapsed` becomes negative at line 1008. The subsequent check at line 1009 (`[[ "$elapsed" -lt "$interval_seconds" ]]`) will always be true, permanently suppressing scans unless `--force` is used.

Add a bounds check after the numeric validation:

 	if ! [[ "$last_run" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then

 		return 0
 	fi

**Add error recovery to `record_scan_timestamp()` to prevent scan failures from persistence errors.**

The `record_scan_timestamp()` function (lines 1021-1025) writes state unconditionally with no error handling. Under `set -euo pipefail`, if `mkdir` or the file write fails (disk full, permission denied, etc.), the entire `cmd_pulse_scan` command fails, converting a successfully completed scan into a failed exit code. This breaks automation expectations.

Wrap the state write with error recovery:
```diff
 record_scan_timestamp() {
 	mkdir -p "$EVOL_STATE_DIR"
 	date +%s >"$EVOL_STATE_FILE"
+	if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then
+		log_warn "Failed to record scan timestamp, but scan completed successfully"
+		return 0
+	fi
 	return 0
 }
```

Alternatively, catch the error and allow graceful degradation, since a completed scan should not be reported as failed when only timestamp persistence fails.

**File**: `.agents/rules/no-hardcoded-secrets.md:3`
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟡 Minor_

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🌐 Web query:

`macOS BSD grep -E support for \s escape sequence ERE`

💡 Result:

` \s ` is **not POSIX ERE**. In POSIX, most backslash escapes other than a small set are *undefined*, so you can’t rely on `grep -E '\s'` being whitespace across platforms. ([gnu.org](https://www.gnu.org/s/emacs/manual/html_node/elisp/POSIX-Regexps.html?utm_source=openai))

On **macOS’s /usr/bin/grep (BSD grep)** specifically:

- macOS’s underlying regex engine documents an **“enhanced”** mode that adds shorthand classes such as `\d`, `\w`, **`\s`**, etc. (see `re_format(7)` “ENHANCED FEATURES”). ([unix.com](https://www.unix.com/man_page/osx/7/re_format/?utm_source=openai))  
- Whether those enhanced escapes work depends on whether the *tool* was built to enable that enhanced mode; it’s not guaranteed just because you used `-E` (extended). ([stackoverflow.com](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12178924/os-x-sed-e-doesnt-accept-extended-regular-expressions?utm_source=openai))

**Portable recommendation (works on macOS BSD grep and everywhere POSIX):**
- Use the POSIX character class instead of `\s`:
  - whitespace: `[[:space:]]`
  - non-whitespace: `[^[:space:]]`

BSD-vs-GNU difference summary: treating `\s` as whitespace is commonly a **GNU grep extension**, and **BSD grep may not** treat it that way—so prefer `[[:space:]]` for portability. ([unix.stackexchange.com](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/617010/why-is-egrep-ignoring-the-negative-whitespace?utm_source=openai))

Citations:

- 1: https://www.gnu.org/s/emacs/manual/html_node/elisp/POSIX-Regexps.html?utm_source=openai
- 2: https://www.unix.com/man_page/osx/7/re_format/?utm_source=openai
- 3: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12178924/os-x-sed-e-doesnt-accept-extended-regular-expressions?utm_source=openai
- 4: https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/617010/why-is-egrep-ignoring-the-negative-whitespace?utm_source=openai

---

🌐 Web query:

`does grep -E support \s on macOS older versions`

💡 Result:

No—on older (and current) macOS, the default `/usr/bin/grep -E` uses **POSIX ERE (BSD grep)**, and `\s` is **not a POSIX ERE escape** (a backslash before an “ordinary” character like `s` is unspecified/undefined in POSIX ERE), so it typically won’t mean “whitespace.” [1]

Use POSIX character classes instead:

```sh
grep -E '[[:space:]]+'    file
grep -E '^[[:space:]]*$'  file
```

If you specifically need `\s`, you generally need **PCRE**, e.g. GNU grep’s PCRE mode:

```sh
ggrep -P '\s+'
```

…but Apple’s BSD `grep` does not provide `-P` by default; you’d install GNU grep (e.g., via Homebrew) to get it. [2]

**Sources:**  
[1] POSIX ERE escapes: backslash before ordinary char is undefined/unspecified (POSIX ERE syntax summary) https://www.classes.cs.uchicago.edu/archive/2013/fall/51025-1/boost_1_50_0/libs/regex/doc/html/boost_regex/syntax/basic_extended.html

  // Use a regex to find all potential tokens with their indices to avoid incorrect index from `indexOf`
  const tokenRegex = /[A-Za-z0-9_\-/.+=]{20,}/g;
  let tokenMatch: RegExpExecArray | null;
  while ((tokenMatch = tokenRegex.exec(text)) !== null) {

        patternName: "high_entropy",
        description: `High-entropy token (${entropy.toFixed(2)} bits/char)`,
        matchedText: token,
        index,
        entropy,
      });
    }
  }

    start = time.time()

**File**: `.agents/scripts/response-scoring-helper.sh:402`
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The SQL query uses multiple correlated subqueries to fetch per-criterion scores. This can be inefficient as it may execute a subquery for each row. A more performant approach is to use a `LEFT JOIN` on the `scores` table and then use conditional aggregation (`MAX(CASE ...)` with `GROUP BY`) to pivot the scores into columns. This will retrieve all the data in a single, more efficient query.

```suggestion
result=$(sqlite3 -separator '|' "$SCORING_DB" "
        SELECT r.model_id, p.category, p.difficulty,
               ${WEIGHTED_AVG_SQL} as weighted_avg,
               r.token_count, r.cost_estimate,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'correctness' THEN s.score END) as corr,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'completeness' THEN s.score END) as comp,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'code_quality' THEN s.score END) as cq,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'clarity' THEN s.score END) as clar
        FROM responses r
        JOIN prompts p ON r.prompt_id = p.prompt_id
        LEFT JOIN scores s ON r.response_id = s.response_id
        WHERE r.response_id = ${response_id}
        GROUP BY r.response_id;
    ")
```

Using `echo` with an unquoted variable (`$*`) can lead to unexpected behavior. If a log message starts with a hyphen (e.g., `-n`), `echo` may interpret it as an option. Additionally, unquoted expansion is subject to word splitting, which can alter spacing within the message. It's safer and more robust to use `printf` with a format string and quoted arguments to ensure messages are printed literally.

```suggestion
printf "[%s] [skill-update] [%s] %s\n" "$timestamp" "$level" "$*" >>"$SKILL_LOG_FILE"
```

The example BigQuery query for reverse lookup uses `technologies LIKE '%React%'`. This is incorrect for two main reasons:

WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM UNNEST(technologies) tech WHERE tech.name = 'React')

![security-critical](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-critical.svg) ![critical](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/critical.svg)

The script is vulnerable to SQL injection. User-provided arguments like `--pr` are used directly in SQL queries without validation. For example, `pr_number` is used on lines 250 and 647. A malicious value like `1; DROP TABLE audit_runs` could be passed.

This vulnerability also exists for the `--run` argument in `cmd_report` (line 869) and `cmd_summary` (line 1017).

**Recommendation:**
Always validate and sanitize user input, especially when it's used in database queries. For numeric IDs, you should verify they are indeed numbers right after parsing them.

Example validation for `pr_number`:
```bash
# After the while loop
if [[ "$pr_number" -ne 0 ]] && ! [[ "$pr_number" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    log_error "Invalid PR number provided: $pr_number"
    return 1
fi
```
Similar checks should be added for `run_id` in `cmd_report` and `cmd_summary`.

### HIGH: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/higgsfield/remotion/render.mjs:79`
![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

There's a logic bug in how a caption's scene index is derived from its `startFrame`. If a caption's `startFrame` occurs after the end of the last scene, it's incorrectly assigned to scene 0 instead of the last scene. This happens because `sceneIdx` is initialized to `0` and is never updated if the `startFrame` is out of bounds of all scenes.

To fix this, you can tentatively update `sceneIdx` on each iteration. This ensures that if the loop completes without finding an earlier match, `sceneIdx` will correctly hold the index of the last scene.

```javascript
    let frameOffset = 0;
    let sceneIdx = 0;
    for (let s = 0; s < scenes.length; s++) {
      sceneIdx = s; // Tentatively assign to current scene
      const sceneDur = (scenes[s].duration || 5) * fps;
      // If start frame is before the end of this scene, we've found our match.
      if ((cap.startFrame || 0) < frameOffset + sceneDur) {
        break;
      }
      frameOffset += sceneDur;

For better performance, the two database queries to get `inbox_count` and `unread_count` can be combined into a single, more efficient query. This reduces the number of separate database connections.

```suggestion
        local inbox_count unread_count

### .agents/scripts/mail-helper.sh (577-581)

                COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'archived' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0)

title: fix: CodeRabbit daily quota exhausted — 15+ PRs blocked from formal review
body:
## Problem

CodeRabbit's daily review quota is exhausted, blocking all open PRs from receiving formal reviews. This prevents the merge pipeline from advancing since the mandatory review-count gate requires at least 1 formal review before merging.

**Evidence:** PR #3725 has 7 comments but 0 formal reviews. CodeRabbit posted:
> You have reached your daily quota limit. Please wait up to 24 hours and I will start processing your requests again!

**Affected PRs (15 in aidevops alone):** #3725, #3720, #3628, #3620, #3618, #3590, #3579, #3545, #3542, #3394, #3324, #3304, #3146, #3106, #3098

**Root cause:** The pulse is creating too many PRs per day, exhausting CodeRabbit's hourly/daily review quota. With 15+ open PRs all created in a short window, the quota is hit before all PRs get reviewed.

## Impact

- All 15 aidevops PRs are blocked from merging
- The merge pipeline is stalled
- Quality-debt PRs accumulate without review

## Proposed fixes

1. **Rate-limit PR creation in the pulse** — add a daily cap on new PRs created per repo (e.g., max 5/day) to stay within CodeRabbit's quota
2. **Batch quality-debt PRs** — instead of one PR per quality-debt issue, batch related issues into a single PR to reduce PR volume
3. **Upgrade CodeRabbit plan** if the current plan's quota is insufficient for the PR volume
4. **Add quota-aware dispatch** — check CodeRabbit quota status before dispatching workers that will create PRs

## Workaround

Wait 24 hours for quota to reset, then the next pulse cycle will find reviews and merge the backlog.

![security-critical](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-critical.svg) ![critical](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/critical.svg)

The `scan_content` function implements a three-layer scanning pipeline where Layer 1 is a keyword pre-filter (`_cs_prefilter`) that skips the entire scan if no suspicious keywords are found. title: t1419: Standalone worker watchdog — auto-detect and kill hung/idle workers
body:
## Problem

When multiple headless workers are dispatched (manually or via pulse), workers that crash, hang, or enter OpenCode's idle-state bug are not automatically detected or cleaned up. The existing watchdog mechanisms in `pulse-wrapper.sh` only monitor the pulse process itself — not independently dispatched workers.

**Observed failure (2026-03-08):** 6 workers dispatched manually, 4 crashed/hung within 5 minutes (thundering herd on MCP cold boot), 1 buffered (API rate limiting), 1 kept working. Required manual consolidation to 1 worker. A second interactive session later hung indefinitely.

## Root Cause

Three failure modes, one systemic gap:

1. **Early crashes (thundering herd):** 6 simultaneous cold boots exhaust RAM (each worker spawns Node.js + language servers + MCP connections). No capacity enforcement for manual dispatch.
2. **Buffering:** Concurrent API calls from same key cause rate-limiting queuing.
3. **Hangs (idle-state bug):** OpenCode enters file-watcher idle state after completing but never exits. Pulse watchdog only covers pulse process, not workers.

## Solution

Create `worker-watchdog.sh` — a standalone launchd service that monitors ALL headless `opencode run` processes:

1. **Extract shared functions** from `pulse-wrapper.sh` into `worker-lifecycle-common.sh` (process age, CPU tree, kill tree)
2. **Create `worker-watchdog.sh`** (~200 lines):
   - Scans all `opencode run` headless processes
   - Three detection signals: CPU idle (5min), progress stall (10min), runtime ceiling (3h)
   - On kill: comment on associated issue, relabel to `status:available`
   - Capacity warnings when total workers exceed MAX_WORKERS
3. **Launchd plist** `sh.aidevops.worker-watchdog.plist` (every 60s, independent of pulse)
4. **Stagger protection** guidance for manual multi-worker dispatch

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `worker-watchdog.sh` detects and kills idle workers within 5 minutes
- [ ] `worker-watchdog.sh` detects and kills stalled workers within 10 minutes
- [ ] Killed workers' issues are re-labelled for re-dispatch
- [ ] `worker-watchdog.sh --install` creates launchd plist
- [ ] `worker-watchdog.sh --status` shows all monitored workers
- [ ] `pulse-wrapper.sh` sources shared functions from `worker-lifecycle-common.sh`
- [ ] ShellCheck clean

title: refactor: standardize on pre-increment ((++var)) across all shell scripts
body:
## Summary

Standardize all shell scripts to use pre-increment `((++var))` instead of post-increment `((var++))` to prevent `set -e` early exit bugs.

## Background

PR #70 fixed a critical bug in `generate-opencode-commands.sh` where `((command_count++))` with `set -e` caused the script to exit when `command_count=0` (post-increment returns the old value, which is 0/falsy, triggering `set -e` exit). CodeRabbit's review (PR #70, issue #3793) identified that this same unsafe pattern exists in 15+ other scripts.

## Scope

Audit found **113 unsafe post-increment patterns** across **50+ scripts** (excluding `for ((...))` loops and patterns already guarded with `|| true`).

Key affected scripts (non-exhaustive):
- `agent-sources-helper.sh` (7 instances)
- `linters-local.sh` (4 instances)
- `pre-commit-hook.sh` (10 instances)
- `beads-sync-helper.sh` (3 instances)
- `site-crawler-helper.sh` (6 instances)
- `aidevops.sh` (12 instances)
- `mcp-register-claude.sh` (6 instances)
- `postflight-check.sh` (2 instances)
- `todo-ready.sh` (6 instances)

## Fix

For each instance, change `((var++))` to `((++var))`. This is safe because:
- Pre-increment returns the new value (always > 0 after first increment)
- Semantically equivalent when the return value isn't used (which is the case for all standalone increment statements)
- `for ((...))` loop increments are NOT affected (they don't trigger `set -e`)

## Notes

- Scripts already using `|| true` guard are safe but should still be migrated for consistency
- Archived scripts (`archived/`) can be skipped
- This was identified as a medium finding in PR #70 review by CodeRabbit

Closes #3793 (partially — the command generator duplication was addressed in a separate PR)

title: t1524: aidevops update deploys CLI but not agents — stale agent detection gap
body:
## Bug Report

### Description

When `aidevops update` is run inside OpenCode (or any environment where `setup.sh --non-interactive` fails silently), the git repo and CLI update successfully but agents at `~/.aidevops/agents/` are not redeployed. The auto-update poller then sees repo=remote and declares "up to date" forever, creating a permanent mismatch.

### Observed Behaviour

- CLI/repo VERSION: 2.170.0
- Deployed agents VERSION: 2.158.0 (12 releases behind)
- `aidevops status` reports "Up to date" (checks repo, not deployed agents)
- Auto-update log: `Already up to date (v2.170.0)` every 10 minutes — never detects stale agents
- User saw changelog and success message during update, but agents were not deployed

### Root Cause (confirmed via code review)

**Two gaps in the update pipeline:**

**1. `cmd_update()` in `aidevops.sh` (line ~744) — no exit code check on setup.sh**

```bash
# Line 724: success message printed BEFORE setup.sh runs
print_success "Updated to version $new_version"
# ...changelog printed...
# Line 744: setup.sh runs, but failure is not caught
bash "$INSTALL_DIR/setup.sh" --non-interactive
# Line 749: cleanup runs regardless
git checkout -- . 2>/dev/null || true
```

The success message and changelog are printed based on `git pull` succeeding, not on agent deployment completing. If `setup.sh` fails, the user sees a false "updated successfully" report.

**2. `cmd_check()` in `auto-update-helper.sh` (line ~903) — no stale-agent detection**

```bash
current=$(get_local_version)   # reads $INSTALL_DIR/VERSION (repo)
remote=$(get_remote_version)   # reads GitHub API
if [[ "$current" == "$remote" ]]; then
    log_info "Already up to date (v$current)"  # never checks deployed agents
    return 0
fi
```

The poller compares repo VERSION vs GitHub API. Once the repo is current, it never checks if `~/.aidevops/agents/VERSION` matches. A failed `setup.sh` creates a permanent mismatch the poller cannot self-heal.

**Note:** `cmd_update()` DOES have stale-agent detection on the "already up to date" path (lines 686-695), so running `aidevops update` a *second* time catches the mismatch. But the user has no reason to re-run an update that reported success.

### Proposed Fix

1. **`cmd_update()` — verify deployment after setup.sh:**
   - Check `setup.sh` exit code
   - After setup.sh runs, compare `$INSTALL_DIR/VERSION` with `~/.aidevops/agents/VERSION`
   - If mismatch, warn the user: "Agent deployment may have failed. Run `./setup.sh` manually from `~/Git/aidevops/`"

2. **`cmd_check()` — add stale-agent detection to the "up to date" path:**
   - After confirming repo=remote, check `~/.aidevops/agents/VERSION`
   - If stale, re-run `setup.sh --non-interactive`
   - Log: "Deployed agents stale ($deployed), re-deploying..."

3. **Move success message after deployment verification** (optional improvement)

### Environment

- Platform: Linux (Ubuntu)
- RAM: 15GB
- aidevops: 2.170.0 (CLI), 2.158.0 (agents)
- Trigger: `aidevops update` run inside OpenCode session

### Files to Modify

- `aidevops.sh`: `cmd_update()` (~line 724-750)
- `.agents/scripts/auto-update-helper.sh`: `cmd_check()` (~line 866-910)

title: ShellCheck memory explosion: circular source chain + stale wrapper missing RSS watchdog

## Bug Report

### Description

ShellCheck processes spawned by the bash-language-server reach 7-14 GB RSS, consuming nearly all RAM on a 15GB machine. The process guard kills them but they regrow within seconds.

### Observed Behaviour

From `~/.aidevops/logs/memory-pressure.log`:

| Timestamp | ShellCheck RSS | Total aidevops RSS |
|-----------|---------------|-------------------|
| Mar 8 13:02 | 7,583 MB | 9,115 MB |
| Mar 9 12:25 | 2,922 MB | — |
| Mar 9 12:27 | 6,653 + 4,343 + 3,584 MB | **14,687 MB** |
| Mar 9 12:28 | **13,974 MB** | 14,220 MB |

Machine: 15 GB RAM, Linux (Ubuntu), ShellCheck 0.11.0

### Root Cause (confirmed via code review + reproduction)

**Three factors combine:**

**1. Circular source chain between `shared-constants.sh` and `config-helper.sh`**

```
shared-constants.sh:1420 → source "$_CONFIG_HELPER"   (config-helper.sh)
config-helper.sh:37      → source "${_CONFIG_HELPER_DIR}/shared-constants.sh"
```

Runtime-safe (include guard `_SHARED_CONSTANTS_LOADED` at shared-constants.sh:14). But ShellCheck is a static analyzer — it doesn't execute guards. When run with `--external-sources` + `--source-path=<scripts-dir>`, ShellCheck follows the cycle infinitely, consuming exponential memory.

Reproduction:
```bash
# Hangs forever, eating all RAM:
shellcheck --external-sources --source-path=~/.aidevops/agents/scripts/ --format=json1 --shell=bash - <<< '#!/bin/bash
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/shared-constants.sh"'

# Safe (wrapper strips --external-sources):
shellcheck --source-path=~/.aidevops/agents/scripts/ --format=json1 --shell=bash - <<< '#!/bin/bash
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/shared-constants.sh"'
# → SC1091 "Not following" — instant, no memory issue
```

**2. bash-language-server hardcodes `--external-sources`** (index.js:82)

The bash-language-server always passes `--external-sources` to ShellCheck. The `shellcheck-wrapper.sh` strips this flag. However, the wrapper may be bypassed:

The language server first reads `SHELLCHECK_PATH` from env (→ wrapper), then calls `connection.workspace.getConfiguration('bashIde')` (server.js:167). If the LSP client (OpenCode) returns `{}` for this section, `ConfigSchema.parse({})` fills Zod defaults including `shellcheckPath: 'shellcheck'` (config.js:38) — overriding the wrapper with the real binary.

**3. Deployed wrapper (v2.158.0) has no RSS watchdog**

The user's agents are stuck at v2.158.0 (see #3980). The v2.158.0 wrapper relies solely on `ulimit -v` for memory limiting. **Confirmed: `ulimit -v` does NOT prevent the explosion on this Linux system** (overcommit_memory=0, ShellCheck survived 15s timeout with 512MB ulimit). The v2.170.0 wrapper has a background RSS watchdog that polls every 2 seconds and kills at 1GB — but it's not deployed.

### Impact

- Near-total RAM exhaustion (14.7 GB / 15 GB)
- Swap thrashing (1.7 GB swap used after events)
- Process guard kills restore stability within ~1 minute, but the cycle repeats
- Affects any OpenCode session where the bash-language-server analyzes scripts that source `shared-constants.sh`

### Proposed Fix (layered)

**Layer 1: Break the circular source chain (root cause)**

Add ShellCheck-visible cycle guard in `config-helper.sh`:

```bash
# Replace line 36-37:
if [[ -z "${_SHARED_CONSTANTS_LOADED:-}" ]]; then
    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
    source "${_CONFIG_HELPER_DIR}/shared-constants.sh" 2>/dev/null || true
fi
```

`# shellcheck source=/dev/null` tells ShellCheck to NOT follow this specific source, breaking the cycle at the static analysis level without affecting runtime behaviour.

**Layer 2: Prevent LSP config override (defense-in-depth)**

Either:
- a) Set `SHELLCHECK_ARGUMENTS` env var to include something that identifies the wrapper is expected (fragile)
- b) Patch the shellcheck-wrapper.sh to also install itself at a PATH location that the default `shellcheck` resolves to (e.g., symlink)
- c) File upstream issue against bash-language-server to not override env-based config with schema defaults

**Layer 3: Agent update (already tracked in #3980)**

Updating agents to v2.170.0 deploys the RSS watchdog wrapper — the most robust mitigation. This is already tracked.

### Files to Modify

- `.agents/scripts/config-helper.sh:36-37` — add `# shellcheck source=/dev/null`
- Optionally: `.agents/scripts/shared-constants.sh:1419` — add `# shellcheck source=/dev/null` (belt and braces)

### Related

- #3980 — Agent update stale (blocks Layer 3 fix)
- GH#2915 — Original ShellCheck memory explosion incident
- PR#2918, PR#2937 — Previous fixes for source-path recursion

### Environment

- Platform: Linux (Ubuntu)
- RAM: 15 GB
- ShellCheck: 0.11.0
- Agents: v2.158.0 (stale, should be v2.170.0)
- bash-language-server: bundled with OpenCode

title: t1424: Zero-config localdev — auto-register projects and `localdev run` wrapper
body:
## Context

Two convenience gaps vs portless that make our localdev stack feel manual:

1. **Manual registration** — user must run `localdev add myapp` before `https://myapp.local` works. portless infers the project name from `package.json`/git automatically.

2. **Manual port passing** — after registration, user must know the assigned port and pass it: `PORT=3100 npm run dev`. portless wraps the command and injects the port automatically.

## What

### `localdev run` command

```bash
# In ~/Git/myapp/ (not yet registered)
localdev run npm run dev
# -> Auto-registers myapp (cert, Traefik route, /etc/hosts, port 3100)
# -> Sets PORT=3100 HOST=0.0.0.0
# -> Runs: npm run dev
# -> https://myapp.local just works

# In a worktree ~/Git/myapp-bugfix-fix-thing/
localdev run npm run dev
# -> Auto-detects worktree, creates branch subdomain
# -> Sets PORT=3101
# -> Runs: npm run dev
# -> https://fix-thing.myapp.local just works
```

### Auto-register on worktree creation

When `localdev_auto_branch()` in `worktree-helper.sh` detects an unregistered project, auto-run `localdev add` before creating the branch route. No manual step needed.

## Subtasks

- [ ] t1424.1 Auto-register in `localdev_auto_branch()` — detect unregistered project, infer name from repo basename or `package.json`, run `localdev add` automatically
- [ ] t1424.2 `localdev run <command>` — wrapper that auto-registers if needed, resolves the correct port (main or branch), sets PORT/HOST env vars, execs the command. Process management: foreground by default, SIGINT/SIGTERM passthrough
- [ ] t1424.3 Update `local-hosting.md` — document `localdev run` as the primary workflow, update Quick Reference and examples

## Why

Closes the zero-config convenience gap with portless without adopting a 3-week-old experimental dependency. Users get `localdev run npm run dev` → named HTTPS URL, same as portless's `portless run npm run dev` but with production-parity Traefik routing, real TLS on port 443, and Docker container support.

Triggered by PR #3996 review discussion.
